note.note:
Consult Summary:
- 45-year-old housekeeper with 3–4 months of painful, cracked, intermittently itchy palmar hand skin worsening to impair work; history strongly suggests occupational contact hand dermatitis; plan includes trigger avoidance (consistent glove use), topical steroid, emollients, and follow-up in 10–14 days.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Painful, cracked skin of the hands, mainly the palms; intermittent itch. Occasional bleeding only after scratching.
- Onset/duration: Began ~3–4 months ago after switching to a hotel housekeeping job.
- Course/severity: Progressive; now painful enough to limit function; missed work for the past 3 days.
- Exacerbating factors: Frequent exposure to cleaning products; inconsistent glove use; wet work (bathrooms).
- Relieving/attempted treatments: OTC emollient (E45) ineffective; oral antihistamine ineffective (names/doses not documented).
- Associated symptoms: Mild generalized dry skin (e.g., legs). States she “doesn’t hydrate much.” Denies fever, nausea, vomiting, bowel or urinary issues. Appetite intact; otherwise feels well.
- Pertinent negatives: No prior diagnosed eczema/dermatitis; no known skin problems historically.

Past Medical History:
- Type 2 diabetes mellitus; no complications discussed.
- No known history of eczema, dermatitis, asthma, or bowel disease.

Medications:
- Metformin (dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Previously tried: E45 emollient; oral antihistamine (names/doses/frequency not documented).
- Allergies: No known drug or general allergies reported.

Social History:
- Occupation: Housekeeper at a hotel (bedrooms, bathrooms); inconsistent glove use with cleaning products.
- Tobacco: Nonsmoker.
- Alcohol: “A couple of pints per week.”
- Work impact: Unable to work for the past 3 days due to hand pain.

Family History:
- Diabetes present in family.
- No known family history of skin disease, asthma, or bowel problems.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not recorded.
- Examination findings: Not recorded.

Investigations:
- None reported/ordered in this encounter.

Assessment & Plan:
- Overall Impression:
  - Likely occupational contact hand dermatitis (predominantly irritant) related to cleaning chemicals and wet work, with superimposed xerosis; diabetes may contribute to dry skin. This aligns with the history and clinician’s impression in the transcript.

- DDx Integration (brief):
  - Irritant contact hand dermatitis (high likelihood): Strong temporal link to new hotel housekeeping role, frequent exposure to cleaning agents, inconsistent glove use, palmar fissuring and pain; antihistamine and simple emollient not helpful.
  - Allergic contact dermatitis (medium likelihood): Possible sensitization to cleaning agents or glove components; pruritus present. Opposing: no clear trigger pattern or classic distribution noted.
  - Asteatotic/xerotic eczema (medium likelihood): Baseline dry skin and diabetes may impair barrier. Opposing: symptoms are most severe on palms and temporally associated with occupational exposures.

- Issue 1: Hand dermatitis (likely contact dermatitis, irritant predominant)
  - Plan:
    - Trigger avoidance: Wear protective gloves consistently during all cleaning tasks; minimize wet work/chemical exposure when possible.
    - Topical steroid cream for inflamed areas (specific agent/dose/route/frequency not documented).
    - Emollient therapy: Apply thicker/“stronger” emollients liberally 3–4 times daily for the next couple of weeks.
    - Safety netting: Return if not improving in 10–14 days, or sooner if worsening/spreading.
    - Prescription to be sent to the patient’s pharmacy as discussed.

- Issue 2: Type 2 diabetes mellitus
  - Plan:
    - Continue current metformin (dose/route/frequency not documented).
    - No changes to diabetes management discussed in this visit.

- Issue 3: Occupational impact
  - Plan:
    - Advised consistent glove use and avoidance of triggers to enable return to work; no additional work accommodations discussed.

- General plan items:
  - Follow-up: Reassess in 10–14 days or earlier if deterioration.

Quality checks:
- Missing but expected elements: No vitals; no physical exam details; specific topical steroid agent and dosing not documented; exact emollient product not documented; laterality not explicitly stated; immunization status not discussed.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx: None noted.
- Transcript quality: Some brief inaudible/unclear segments; overall history adequate.
